seoTitle: Build a Website Using Google Workspace's Google Sites
metaDescription: Create a professional website with Google Sites through your Google Workspace account, no coding needed, with drag-and-drop editing and easy publishing.
intro: Google Workspace includes Google Sites, a free drag-and-drop website builder that lets you create a site for a business, portfolio, or internal team without writing any code. This guide walks through opening Sites from your Workspace apps, building a page with the actual editor panel, configuring viewer settings, and publishing with a working web address. It's suited to small businesses, freelancers, and teams who want a fast, cloud-hosted site using tools already included in their Workspace plan.

steps.heading: Open Google Sites from your Workspace apps
steps.body: Google Sites isn't a separate purchase — it's one of the apps sitting in the Google Workspace app grid alongside Groups, YouTube, Maps, Photos, Translate, and others accessible from the Admin Console or the app launcher. Click the Sites icon to jump straight into the builder rather than searching for a standalone Sites website, which can be confusing the first time since it's easy to overlook among the dozens of other Workspace app icons in that grid.

image.caption: The Workspace app grid, with the Sites icon sitting among Groups, YouTube, Maps, News, Photos, and other Google apps.

steps.heading: Start a new project and learn the editor layout
steps.body: A new site opens as an untitled "Project" with a placeholder hero section reading "Project Name" and a one-line description over a full-width image. The right-hand panel is where you'll spend most of your time, split into Insert, Pages, and Themes tabs — Insert gives you Text box, Images, Embed, and Drive buttons up top, plus a scrollable gallery of pre-built content block layouts below that combine images and text in different arrangements. Everything autosaves, shown by a small "Saving..." indicator near the Publish button, so there's no separate save step to remember.

image.caption: The Sites editor on a new project, with the Insert panel's Text box, Images, Embed, and Drive options plus a gallery of content block layouts.

steps.heading: Build out pages and drop in embedded content
steps.body: Click any content block to add it to the page, then drag it into position — this is the drag-and-drop part that removes the need for any code. Beyond the basic Insert options, the same panel's lower sections give you dedicated buttons for Calendar, Map, YouTube, Docs, Slides, Sheets, and Forms, so embedding a booking calendar, a business location, a video, or a contact form is a matter of clicking the icon and pointing it at the right file or address rather than pasting embed code by hand.

steps.heading: Configure viewer tools and site settings
steps.body: Open Settings from the toolbar to reach five tabs: Navigation, Brand images, Viewer tools, Analytics, and Announcement banner. Viewer tools controls small but meaningful details — an info icon toggle for showing when a page was last updated and a contact-form shortcut, plus an anchor links toggle that lets visitors hover over headings to link directly to a specific section of a long page. These settings save automatically and apply the next time you publish, so you can adjust them at any point without republishing immediately.

image.caption: The Settings panel's Viewer tools tab, with toggles for the info icon's last-updated time, contact form, and anchor links.

steps.heading: Publish your site and set its web address
steps.body: Click Publish in the top-right corner to open the "Publish your site" dialog. Here you set the Web address portion of your URL — Sites checks availability as you type and shows a green checkmark once it's valid — which combines with your Workspace domain to form the live link, for example sites.google.com/yourcompany.com/yoursitename. A "Who can view my site" section underneath lets you restrict access to just your organization or open it publicly, with a Manage link to fine-tune permissions before you commit.

image.caption: The Publish your site dialog, with the web address field, a live URL preview, and viewer-access controls before publishing.

steps.heading: Point a fully custom domain at your site, if you need one
steps.body: The default sites.google.com address works fine for an internal team page or a quick portfolio, but a customer-facing business site usually wants its own domain, like www.yourbusiness.com instead. That requires a separate custom domain mapping step done through Google Domains or your third-party registrar, which involves verifying domain ownership and adding DNS records Google provides — it isn't part of the Publish dialog itself, so budget extra time for DNS propagation, which can take anywhere from a few minutes to a day depending on your registrar.

faq.question: Do I need coding skills to build a site with Google Sites?
faq.answer: No — the editor works entirely through drag-and-drop content blocks and dedicated Insert buttons for text, images, and embeds like Calendar, Maps, and Forms, with no code required.

faq.question: Can I use my own domain name with Google Sites?
faq.answer: Yes, but it's a separate step from publishing. The Publish dialog sets your sites.google.com web address; a fully custom domain needs to be mapped through Google Domains or a third-party registrar with DNS verification.

faq.question: Is Google Sites included with my Google Workspace plan?
faq.answer: Yes — Sites appears directly in the Workspace app grid alongside tools like Gmail, Drive, and Calendar, with no additional cost or separate signup.

faq.question: Can I embed things like YouTube videos or Google Forms?
faq.answer: Yes — the Insert panel includes dedicated buttons for Calendar, Map, YouTube, Docs, Slides, Sheets, and Forms, so you point them at the content you want rather than pasting embed code manually.

faq.question: Can multiple team members work on the same site?
faq.answer: Yes — the "Who can view my site" section in the Publish dialog includes a Manage link for controlling access, and since Sites lives in Drive, standard Workspace sharing and collaboration permissions apply.
